title: The Last Gas the Blood Touches

scenes.visual: Title card 'The Last Gas the Blood Touches' fades in over a side view of a trout beside a cartoon human chest, 16:9. COLOUR MAP, same in every scene and in the second film: water or air = BLUE arrows and BLUE stream; blood = RED arrows and RED stream; oxygen = small GOLD dots riding in each stream, their density showing the oxygen partial pressure within that stream only (dense = high, sparse = low), with the PO2 value as on-screen text; dot density never stands for total oxygen per litre, which appears only as a separate 'oxygen per litre' bar; carbon dioxide = small PURPLE dots; diffusion across the barrier = thin GOLD arrows for oxygen, PURPLE arrows for carbon dioxide; the barrier = a GREY strip. Labels on screen use the symbols PO2, PCO2, deltaP (shown as the Greek capital delta then P), A, T. Cartoon schematics only, no molecular structures; any curve or bar not computed is labelled 'schematic'. Numbers appear only as on-screen text.

scenes.tts: Water holds far less oxygen than air. Yet a trout's gill can send its blood out at a higher oxygen partial pressure than the water leaving it. Your lung cannot do that with air. Why not?
scenes.visual: Left: a cartoon trout; a BLUE stream of water enters its mouth and leaves under the gill cover. Right: a cartoon human chest; BLUE air flows in and out of the mouth. Below, two 'oxygen per litre' bars: 'air' tall, 'water' short, label 'air-saturated fresh water, 15-20 C: about 30 times less oxygen per litre'. Question card: 'Why can a gill do what a lung cannot?'
scenes.narration: Water holds far less oxygen than air. Yet a trout's gill can send its blood out at a higher oxygen partial pressure than the water leaving it. Your lung cannot do that with air. Why not?

scenes.tts: Each gas in a mixture has a partial pressure, its share of the total pressure. Dry air at sea level is about one fifth oxygen. But partial pressure is not amount. Water left touching air reaches the same oxygen partial pressure. Yet each litre holds far less oxygen.
scenes.visual: A tall bar labelled 'total pressure, dry air at sea level: about 760 mmHg' splits into coloured slices; the GOLD oxygen slice (about a fifth of the bar) slides out and is labelled '21% oxygen' then 'PO2 about 160 mmHg'. The word 'partial pressure = one gas's share of the total' types out beneath. Then a BLUE water layer under the air: two PO2 gauges, air and water, read the same ('same PO2'), while beside them the 'oxygen per litre' bars from the opening stay tall for air and short for water. Label: 'partial pressure is not amount'.
scenes.narration: Each gas in a mixture has a partial pressure, its share of the total pressure. Dry air at sea level is about one fifth oxygen. But partial pressure is not amount. Water left touching air reaches the same oxygen partial pressure. Yet each litre holds far less oxygen.

scenes.tts: Oxygen crosses an exchange surface only by diffusion. Molecules cross both ways, but the net flow runs from higher partial pressure to lower. So here, richer means higher partial pressure, not more oxygen.
scenes.visual: Close-up of one GREY barrier strip, BLUE water above with dense GOLD dots, RED blood below with sparse GOLD dots. A few faint GOLD arrows cross upward, many bold GOLD arrows cross downward, from dense to sparse; a net arrow points down. A small 'no pump' icon (a crossed-out pump) sits on the strip. Label: 'net diffusion: high PO2 to low PO2'.
scenes.narration: Oxygen crosses an exchange surface only by diffusion. Molecules cross both ways, but the net flow runs from higher partial pressure to lower. So here, richer means higher partial pressure, not more oxygen.

scenes.tts: Fick's law gives three dials for speed. More area, a steeper partial pressure difference and a thinner barrier all speed transfer. That is why gills and lungs are large and thin. They are moist because gases must dissolve before crossing cells.
scenes.visual: Three labelled dials under the strip: 'A, area', 'deltaP, partial-pressure difference', 'T, barrier thickness'. Turning the area dial widens the strip; the difference dial makes the gap between dense and sparse GOLD dots larger; the thickness dial thins the GREY strip. Each turn thickens the GOLD transfer arrows. On screen: 'rate = k x A x deltaP / T'. Then quick cut-outs: a feathery gill filament and a cluster of alveoli, labelled 'large, thin'; a thin water film appears on each surface, labelled 'moist: gases dissolve before crossing cells'.
scenes.narration: Fick's law gives three dials for speed. More area, a steeper partial pressure difference and a thinner barrier all speed transfer. That is why gills and lungs are large and thin. They are moist because gases must dissolve before crossing cells.

scenes.tts: Here, all along the surface, the water or air stays richer than the blood beside it. Diffusion brings the blood toward it, never past. So the leaving blood can at best reach the partial pressure it last touched.
scenes.visual: The RED blood stream runs under the BLUE medium along the strip; at every point a small PO2 tag shows the medium above the blood (label: 'medium richer than blood all along'). The blood exits the right end. A dashed horizontal line marks the PO2 of the BLUE medium at the exact spot where the blood leaves; the blood's PO2 gauge rises toward it and stops just below. Label: 'ceiling = PO2 of the last water or air touched (while the medium stays richer)'. A small gauge 'how close: Fick and the flows' sits beside it.
scenes.narration: Here, all along the surface, the water or air stays richer than the blood beside it. Diffusion brings the blood toward it, never past. So the leaving blood can at best reach the partial pressure it last touched.

scenes.tts: Run water and blood the same way along a thin gill plate, a lamella. The water starts rich and the blood starts poor. Partway along, their partial pressures close in on each other. The rest of the plate adds little.
scenes.visual: A long lamella, BLUE water flowing left to right on top, RED blood flowing left to right below. GOLD dot density in the water falls and in the blood rises; a computed pair of curves (linear exchanger model, same-direction flow, finite area) traces both PO2 values along the length, approaching each other and flattening by the middle without ever meeting or crossing. The flattened part is shaded and labelled 'adds little'. At the right end, the leaving blood's gauge sits just below the leaving water's.
scenes.narration: Run water and blood the same way along a thin gill plate, a lamella. The water starts rich and the blood starts poor. Partway along, their partial pressures close in on each other. The rest of the plate adds little.

scenes.tts: Now reverse the blood, so it runs against the water. Where will the leaving blood end up?
scenes.visual: The RED arrows in the lower stream swing round to point right to left. The two curves vanish. Question card: 'Blood against the water: where does the leaving blood end up?'
scenes.narration: Now reverse the blood, so it runs against the water. Where will the leaving blood end up?

scenes.visual: Question card holds over the reversed lamella; a small timer ring fills.

scenes.tts: The blood about to leave meets water that has just arrived. All along the plate, the water stays a little richer than the blood beside it. This is countercurrent exchange.
scenes.visual: Computed curves (on-screen label: 'linear exchanger; equal oxygen-carrying flows of water and blood; large area'): water PO2 falls from left to right, blood PO2 rises from right to left, the two lines parallel with a steady gap. Small GOLD arrows cross the strip along its whole length. The leaving blood (left end) sits close to the incoming water; its gauge is higher than the gauge of the water leaving at the right end. Label: 'countercurrent'.
scenes.narration: The blood about to leave meets water that has just arrived. All along the plate, the water stays a little richer than the blood beside it. This is countercurrent exchange.

scenes.tts: With a large, thin surface, the leaving blood can beat the water leaving. Running the same way, it never could.
scenes.visual: Same countercurrent lamella; the area and thickness dials from earlier sit beside it. As area is turned up and the strip thins, the leaving blood's gauge (left end) rises above the gauge of the water leaving (right end); a small inset of the same-direction plate shows its blood exit gauge stuck just below its water exit gauge. Labels: 'countercurrent: blood can beat the water leaving' and 'same direction: never'.
scenes.narration: With a large, thin surface, the leaving blood can beat the water leaving. Running the same way, it never could.

scenes.tts: Fold the surface into a dead-ended sac, an alveolus in a mammal lung. Air goes in and out by the same tube. Each breath only partly renews the gas inside.
scenes.visual: The GREY strip curls up into a round sac on the end of a tube: label 'alveolus'. BLUE air enters and leaves through the same tube; only part of the sac's gas is replaced each breath, shown as a fresh BLUE swirl mixing into a paler pool.
scenes.narration: Fold the surface into a dead-ended sac, an alveolus in a mammal lung. Air goes in and out by the same tube. Each breath only partly renews the gas inside.

scenes.tts: Blood keeps taking oxygen out. So the sac's gas sits well below the inhaled air. Every capillary touches that same mixed gas. Blood can at best match it.
scenes.visual: RED capillaries wrap the sac; GOLD arrows leave the sac gas into each capillary. On-screen gauges: 'warmed, humidified inhaled air: about 150 mmHg' and 'alveolar gas: about 100 mmHg (resting adult human)'. Each capillary's exit gauge rises to the alveolar line and no further. Label: 'ventilated pool'.
scenes.narration: Blood keeps taking oxygen out. So the sac's gas sits well below the inhaled air. Every capillary touches that same mixed gas. Blood can at best match it.

scenes.tts: That answers the trout. In its gill, the leaving blood last touches fresh, incoming water. In your lung, it last touches stale, mixed gas.
scenes.visual: Split screen: left, the countercurrent lamella with its leaving blood beside incoming BLUE water, highlighted; right, the alveolus with its capillaries inside the pale mixed pool, highlighted. Labels: 'last touched: incoming water' and 'last touched: mixed alveolar gas'.
scenes.narration: That answers the trout. In its gill, the leaving blood last touches fresh, incoming water. In your lung, it last touches stale, mixed gas.

scenes.tts: Fick's law and the flows of blood and water or air set how close the blood gets. The flow arrangement sets what it last touches. Breathing keeps that water or air fresh.
scenes.visual: Three stacked cards appear one by one beside a small strip diagram: 'Fick and the flows: how close (A, deltaP, T)', 'arrangement: what blood last touches', 'breathing: keeps it fresh'. The strip's RED exit gauge sits just under the dashed ceiling line.
scenes.narration: Fick's law and the flows of blood and water or air set how close the blood gets. The flow arrangement sets what it last touches. Breathing keeps that water or air fresh.

scenes.visual: Hex end card. Take-home line: 'Blood gaining oxygen can at best reach the PO2 it last touched.'
